chapter-1-brain-map/chapter-one-brain-ma.title: Chapter One Brain Map
chapter-1-brain-map/chapter-one-brain-ma.description: Three Specific ContextsPg. 9-12Chapter 1 - Theories of Development & GeneticsTheories of DevelopmentMultidirectional - We don't just grow in one area, and we don't just stay at a standstill either. Humans can grow in multiple areas, in one area, or actually decay or have loss as well.Lifelong - You don't reach 28 years old and stay stuck like that forever. You grow in some ways, lose other things (coughmalepatterbaldnesscoughcough), and that means you can become a totally different individual at 86 or something.Multidimensional: We can change across three different domains or dimensions (not literal); physical, cognitive, and psychosocial.Characterized by Plasticity - How we can accept change basicallyMultidisciplinary - Double Dipping in the party dip but in a Human Development lens. He basically recognizes that people can take multiple perspectives into account.Normative history-graded influences: The period of time in which you were born can have a great deal of importance to your individual characteristics (ex. Baby Boomers -> Talk on Phone, Gen Z -> Life is Phone)Normative age-graded influences: An age grade means stages like toddler or teenagerNon-normative life influences:MulticontextualPsychosocial - How we interact with those around us.Cognitive - Changes in our minds, like learning a new language, or taking a Human Development class :)All three of these Domains interact with each other and change one another. Failure in one can cause others to faulter, and the inverse is also applicable.Physical - Biological development (puberty, major illness).Socioeconomic status is also another context, but Paul Baltes didn't feel like adding it in his list I guess. Socioeconomic just means your place in society and tax brackets (businessman vs ceo) also has an effect on your development.

chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/behav.title: Behavioral Genetics
chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/behav.description:
Behavioral Genetics measure how much of a person's traits are from genes and predisposition, versus how much is from their environment and opportunities (or lack thereof), essentially nature v nurture.
Passive genotype-environment correlation - A child is born into a family that supports athleticism while being naturally athletic. Basically both support a trait.
Evocative genotype-environment correlation - How individual characteristics (being shy, being extroverted, or being unendingly hungry) changes how an environment reacts to them.
Active genotype-environment correlation - natural predisposition to things or natural ability causing people to seek out specific environments to reinforce certain characteristics.
Genotype - Environment Interactions - The inverse of the aforementioned AGEC, where the environment enforces or breaks inherited characteristics.
Epigenetics - The changing of genes themselves due to environmental aspects.

chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/genes.title: Genes
chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/genes.description: Genes are sequences of nucleotides, blueprints for making proteins. Proteins then construct cells and command the functions of them. Genes are located in chromosomes, and there are 20,500 genes in the human body (est.) People gain 23 chromosomes per parent, adding to a total of 46. There are two main aspects of genes are Genotype and Phenotype. When a child inherits too many or too little chromosomes, it's called chromosomal abnormality. This is usually linked to an older mother, as the ovum has been been aged for longer and has a higher chance to mutate. The most common example of chromosomal abnormality is down syndrome.

chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/genot.title: Genotype
chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/genot.description: Quite simply the sum total of genes a person inherits. I don't know if they're more complicated than that.

chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/meios.title: Meiosis
chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/meios.description: The process in which the sexual reproduction cells go through duplication and copy themselves. The first duplication creates a perfect copy, but then they split apart and only have half the genetic material of the original cell.

chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/mitos.title: Mitosis
chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/mitos.description: The process in which cells go through duplication and copy themselves. The nucleus of the cell contains the chromosomes of the human, and when going through mitosis they replicate and double perfectly. The the cell splits an creates two identical copies.

chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/pheno.title: Phenotype
chapter-2-brain-map/notes-detailed/pheno.description: Phenotypes are the expressed features of a gene. There are dominant genes, where the phenotype they present is presented even when paired with a different version of the gene, and there are recessive genes, where they don't present themselves unless paired with another recessive. These different versions of genes come from having a mix of chromosomes from your mother and father, and when you have the same version of a gene, that called being homozygous, and being different means heterozygous. Different versions of the same genes are called alleles. Most characteristics or phenotypes are polygenic, meaning it's a collaborative effort from multiple genes for the presented phenotype.

chapter-3-brain-map/notes-detailed/nutri.title: Nutrition
chapter-3-brain-map/notes-detailed/nutri.description: Nutrition is arguably one of, if not the most important part of a child's early development. Without a proper food source, infants go through marasmus (starvation due to lack of calories and protein), and go through muscle, fat, and eventually life loss. Kwashiorkor (sounds like it should be a [Noble Phantasm](noble phantasm - Google Search)), or the disease of the displaced child, and this often takes place after infants are weaned off but don't get enough protein in their diet. Malnutrition is a growing concern, especially when it's put into the parameters of children, they're our future after all, and numerous efforts have been made to help aide people starving throughout the world.In a less gloomy note, breastmilk is apparently the bomb, just like Lightning McQueen (if you don't understand that reference, please go watch Cars 2 NOW). Breast milk is more cost efficient, it does a better job at immunizing infant's than formula, and it actually reduces health risk in the mother! Children are typically weaned off slowly at 4-6 months, and are taken off breast milk at around 1-2 years of age.

chapter-3-brain-map/notes-detailed/overa.title: Overall Brain Development
chapter-3-brain-map/notes-detailed/overa.description: We are actually born with most of our neurons, around 85 billion (ok but would they win against 1 of every Pokemon?), and they go through maturation over time. As more connections are formed, over and over again, they begin to help the formation of the early brain's structure.The infant brain itself actually grows in size, with it becoming 55% the size of the adult brain at 90 days after birth. Keep in mind (heh pun intended) that the child is still around 10 pounds during this age, so this is mind boggling (again, see what I did there).The brain does actually mature at different rates with different parts during this age, with the the primary motor areas developing at a much faster pace than the sensory areas. Along with that, the prefrontal cortex is the least developed.
chapter-3-brain-map/notes-detailed/overa.sourcePath: Chapter 3 Brain Map/Notes Detailed/Overall Brain Development.md

chapter-3-brain-map/notes-detailed/overa.title: Overall Physical Growth
chapter-3-brain-map/notes-detailed/overa.description: Infants at a young age go through enormous changes over the course of around 24 months. They start out being basically blind, small, and having about half of their total body being nothing but head, to a normal (hopefully), functioning person within only a two decade period. That's like going from small hairless lemur to a normal person in the same timeframe in a way. Newborns range from 5-10 pound at birth, and are around 20 inches in length. They actually lose 5 percent of their body weight as they adjust to being out of the womb (kind of jealous I'm not gonna lie). This weight loss is then subsequently followed by a rapid growth spurt (again, jelly), and begins to gain about double it's weight in 4 months, and triple in 12. At 2 y/o, they can weigh about 20-40 lbs., and are about 5 Bud Light cans tall, give or take a few bottle caps.While sharing was always well developed, it becomes a little bit better and babies often forma connection with their mother's voice. 5 of the 6 sense actually for some sort of connection with the mother. After children are born, they have absolutely terrible eyesight, even worse than mine (and that's saying something), and yet over the course for their growth, they grow accustomed to their mother's face and even look out for it. Infant's like the taste of their mother, and even grow to love their smell. Babies also love to be coddled by their mother's (I can actually personally verify this).Babies also grow through their cute wittwe feet aww, and they learn how to walk bipedally over time. This however is a very long process, so they will typically be able to independently walk around 2 years after birth. In addition, babies do not have fine motor control in their hands, but over the course of 9 moths they build up to grab things with their forefinger and thumb, like a crab in human flesh!!!Nutrition

chapter-3-brain-map/notes-detailed/piage.title: Piaget
chapter-3-brain-map/notes-detailed/piage.description:
Piaget believed that our main drive to improve ourselves was balance, where upon trying to reach balance, we organize information into framework, known as schema.
His theory of development started out with the sensorimotor stage as a child. When a child is confronted with something new, they either go through Assimilation or Accommodation. Through Piaget's eyes, infants, learn the world through their motor skills and visual senses.
This is the sensorimotor stage: Reflexes: Newborns learn about the world with the base instincts and reflexes we're born with (ex. sucking and reaching). PCR: The child uses the body to do a repeated activity. They may find an action and find it interesting, which motivates them to do it again and again until the new behavior is learned. SCR: The child starts interacting with things in their environment, and then through making repeated contact begins to form new behaviors. This makes them more engaged with the outside world, and taking delight in making things happen through their own actions. CSCR: The infant combines their reflexes and behaviors and goes to achieve a specific goal in mind. They begin to be able to have thoughts and carrying out goal-directed activity. TCR: The toddler begins to experiment and explore the word with a trial and error approach, trying to see what happens and responding accordingly. This uses both cognitive thinking, and motor skills. BRT: The periods ends, and the child gains symbolic thought. Objects can be seen as symbols, and the child can use mental strategies to solve problems. They also are able to pretend play, and remember and repeat things they've seen or heard.Up next, we have the preoperational stage. From the ages of 2-7, "children use symbols to represent words, images, and ideas..." (The Textbook). Preoperational means that children can't take information and manipulate it logically, like separating things based on personal perspective. An example I can take from my own life is when I was a child, I thought the bigger slice of cake, the more cake was present, even though the same cake might be cut differently and still had the same amount of cake. Symbolic Function: Between the ages 2 and 4, this stage focuses on how the child is able to mentally represent objects and uses perception when problem solving. Like how many dish soaps does Johnny have (some ball knowledge is needed for that reference). Intuitive Thought: This substage focuses on the growth of being able to use intuitive thinking more than perception. So now we're working with imaginary dish soaps. This is also the inquisitive age, you know, where the kid asks a bajillion questions to arrive to their own conclusion, and if you're the parent, you're just hoping that they eventually get the right thing down eventually.

chapter-4-brain-map/notes-detailed/child.title: Child Abuse
chapter-4-brain-map/notes-detailed/child.description:
"The Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act (United States Department of Health and Human
Services, 2013) defines Child Abuse and Neglect as: Any recent act or failure to act on the part
of a parent or caretaker which results in death, serious physical or emotional harm, sexual
abuse or exploitation; or an act or failure to act, which presents an imminent risk of serious
harm (p. viii)." (The Textbook)There are four major types of maltreatment, which include neglect, sexual and physical abuse, and psychological maltreatment, and they can also occur concurrently.Honestly I don't think I'll physically note anything here because I'm uncomfortable with the subject, and honestly reading it has more or less ingrained it into my head. So just trust me bro, I read the entire thing a few times.(Super side note, the textbook says that kids experiencing high stress can reduce the size of the hippocampus leading to memory problems, and even lead to reduced disease immunity. I don't like how accurate this is to me as a child who experienced high stress.)

chapter-4-brain-map/notes-detailed/gende.title: Gender
chapter-4-brain-map/notes-detailed/gende.description:
"Gender is the cultural, social and psychological meanings associated with masculinity and feminity (Spears Brown & Jewell, 2018). A person’s sense of self as a member of a particular gender is known as gender identity. The development of gender identity appears to be due to an interaction among biological, social and representational influences (Ruble, Martin, & Berenbaum, 2006). Gender roles, or the expectations associated with being male or female, are learned in one’s culture throughout childhood and into adulthood." (The Textbook)Gender during early childhood is characterized by the culture you are part of, and the interaction the child has with other's during that time period. For example, an "atomic family" may dictate that a boy should go out and play with the dog, or go and play with the other boys of the neighborhood. The girl, in contrast, should stay at home and knit or whatever. Meanwhile, other cultures might have different expectations of your gender when growing up, and will treat you as such, or they might be of a culture where gender isn't as important. Either way, the way we are treated (Gender Roles) is heavily impacted by those in close proximity AKA Gender Socialization.The social learning theory dictates that we learn our gender through observing the world around us, and pick up on the traits associated for our gender through modeling and conditioning. This theory dictates that we learn what it means to be our gender, and the rules we have to follow.The gender schema theory states that we pick and choose our gender based on what we like, as if it were a super saiyan bargain sale. This is meant to be where the children actively seek out in improvement for their own gender, and choosing an ideal self through gender. "Boys do A, that's cool, I wan to be a boy.""Developmental intergroup theory states that many of our gender stereotypes are so strong
because we emphasize gender so much in culture (Bigler & Liben, 2007). Developmental
intergroup theory postulates that adults’ heavy focus on gender leads children to pay attention to
gender as a key source of information about themselves and others, to seek out any possible
gender differences, and to form rigid stereotypes based on gender that are subsequently difficult
to change." (The Textbook)Many young children don't conform to gender roles, and some may even actively reject one sex's associations (ie clothes, toys, anatomy) in favor of the opposite sex's. The textbook stresses that gender is something that should be celebrated and supported.
On a personal note, I don't understand how it could ever be negatively looked upon, as most American gender roles that are expressed at that age don't really matter ethically speaking. A child could do whatever they want, they're still your kid, and you have a responsibility towards them. The stress in the textbook about toys and clothes are also of note, because it's an economic angle, which pushes into question whether or not the reason stress on gender based toys is a means to generate more money.

chapter-4-brain-map/notes-detailed/media.title: Media
chapter-4-brain-map/notes-detailed/media.description:
Television has evolved fast since it's conception, to the point where it's unrecognizable and the industry has grown so much from there to where we are here. Children's television has been a growing industry for years now, with networks like PBS Kids and Nickelodeon as recent examples. Children actually don't learn well from television for the first 5 years of life, with studies suggesting a caregiver explained what the takeaway is from what they just watched. As we move on into the future more and more, it's encouraged to have less screen time, and more time socializing to help gain their hands on experience and exploration.
If I ever am lucky enough to have a kid, I'm not letting them anywhere near a smart device for themselves. They can have a school device maybe, but until they're a more responsible age, like 10 or 12, they won't get something they just have free access to like that. A recreational device is a guarantee though, I would just set up parental controls on everything. Ideally however, they wouldn't need to balance, as I would be there to help them and to give my own blend of entertainment/lessons.

chapter-4-brain-map/notes-detailed/spank.title: Spanking
chapter-4-brain-map/notes-detailed/spank.description: Spanking has been noted as a rite of passage in the textbook, or rather as thought to be a rite of passage. The textbook (and I'm summarizing/paraphrasing) goes into detail how many people spank, and how it has a high correlation value with aggression and rule breaking. When father were the one spanking, children actually had a higher correlation value, and the whole study the textbook covers shows that spanking can have negative effects, not positive ones. Though I'm curious whether or not the prefaces of the study as a whole (it's late, I have no idea whether or not prefaces is the right word here) have any attribution towards it. For example, did the parent explain the reason behind the spanking? Was there a combination of spanking with other punishments? How about stretching out the spankings so that it's not TWO TIMES per week. I'm not trying to advocate for spanking, per say, but I'm curious whether or not the study bothered to look into those details, because I feel those can have a big effect on whether the true lesson takes hold, or the child interperets the use of physical force as a simple message of anger or hate.

I guess it also changes things when our personalities are so laid back, but the worst scuffles we got into were because we simply wanted to fight one another. Boys, huh? info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.

info_allowResizing.description: Whether or not to allow the sidebars to be resized

info_allowCollapsing.description: Whether or not to allow the sidebars to be collapsed

info_rightDefaultWidth.description: The default width of the right sidebar

info_leftDefaultWidth.description: The default width of the left sidebar

info_selector.description: CSS selector for an element. The feature will be placed relative to this element.

info_type.description: Will this feature be placed before, after, or inside (at the beggining or end).

info_featurePlacement.description: Where to place this feature on the page. (Relative to the selector)

info_sourcePath.description: The local path to the source .html file which will be included.

info_allowFoldingLists.description: Whether or not to allow lists to be folded

info_allowFoldingHeadings.description: Whether or not to allow headings to be folded

info_siteUrl.description: The url that this site will be hosted at

info_authorName.description: The name of the author of the site

bodyClasses: publish css-settings-manager styled-scrollbars show-inline-title show-ribbon is-focused
